proposals.title: Pause flow #3 (Finance weekly pack)? Its source machine FIN-02 has an urgent case open.
Mark C:\Finance\Payroll on FIN-02 as restricted? Files from there were gathered and sent out.
Ask the Operations Admin to follow up on OPS-03 (files renamed to one odd ending)?

tell.1:
On Sunday 18 October at {t:12:00}, with {p:Kofi} signed in on {m:FIN-02}, the payroll spreadsheet {f:payroll-q3.xlsx} was opened. Three minutes later it was moved into the Windows Temp folder under a new name, {f:notes.txt.dll}, so that it looks like a piece of Windows rather than a spreadsheet, and then it was hidden. In the same minute fourteen files from the Payroll folder, eight of them restricted, were copied into a Staging folder and packed into {f:q3.zip}. At {t:12:06} a USB drive was plugged in, and the archive was copied onto it. A minute later the archive was deleted from the machine, and at {t:12:08} the list of recent files was cleared. It all took about eight minutes, and every step came from programs Kofi had started.

What makes it serious is what was carried, not the drive it went on: eight of the fourteen files are restricted, and they left the machine disguised and packed, with the traces wiped behind them. The same files on a drive Kofi uses every day would be just as serious, and harmless files on a brand new drive would not have raised a case at all.
tell.2:
At {t:12:43} on Sunday 18 October, with {p:Yaw} signed in on {m:OPS-03}, a program began renaming the documents in the Documents folder. In under two minutes thirty of them, starting with {f:doc0.docx}, had .locked added to their names, far faster than anyone could do by hand. None of them was opened or edited first; only the names changed.

This is how ransomware usually begins: the files are locked and renamed so their owner can no longer open them. A migration or conversion tool started on purpose would look the same, so it is worth asking Yaw whether they ran anything just before a quarter to one.
tell.3:
At {t:09:53} on Sunday 18 October, on {m:OPS-06} where {p:Kwame} was signed in, the restricted spreadsheet {f:payroll-q3.xlsx} was moved into the Windows Temp folder and renamed {f:notes.txt.dll}, so it passes for a part of Windows. A minute later it was hidden.

At {t:09:56}, three minutes after it began, the machine stopped reporting to Falcon while it was still switched on, and it has not been heard from since. A laptop lid closing or a network fault would explain the silence, but not a restricted file being disguised and hidden just before it.
tell.4:
Between {t:08:15} and {t:08:20} on Sunday 18 October, {p:Nana} opened fifteen documents on {m:OPS-05}, starting with {f:doc0.docx}, spread across four folders of the HR share that have nothing to do with their own work.  Nothing was copied, changed or taken anywhere; the files were only opened, one after another, in five minutes.

On its own it is mild. Nana may have been covering for a colleague or hunting for one particular file, and Detective has kept it in view rather than raising it.
tell.5:
Early on Sunday 18 October, at {t:05:48}, {p:Afi} opened the restricted spreadsheet {f:payroll-q3.xlsx} in {g:Excel} on {m:FIN-01}. Over the next two minutes a picture of the whole screen was taken four times while it was open, each one put on the clipboard, ready to be pasted somewhere else.

One screenshot is ordinary. Four in a row of a restricted payroll sheet, at ten to six in the morning, is what calls for a look. Afi may have been capturing their own work or showing a problem to support, and nothing so far shows the pictures leaving the machine.
tell.6:
On Saturday 26 September at {t:06:19}, three spreadsheets from the Finance payroll folder, {f:r0.xlsx}, {f:r1.xlsx} and {f:r2.xlsx}, were copied into a folder called Misc on {m:LOG-01}, where {p:Esi} signs in. They sat there untouched for three weeks. On Saturday 17 October at {t:17:19} they were packed into {f:misc.zip}, and a minute later the archive was copied onto a USB drive.

None of the three spreadsheets is restricted, so what was carried is not alarming on its own, and the drive being new to this machine says nothing either way. The case is open because files from the Finance payroll folder ended up on a logistics machine and then left it. Nothing has been deleted or cleared since, which fits an honest transfer; if Esi had a reason to be working on them, it is explained.
tell.7:
At {t:11:20} on Saturday 17 October, {f:contract-amendment-7.docx} was deleted from the Legal folder on {m:OPS-01} while {p:Kojo} was signed in. It was a single file, deleted in one go, with nothing unusual before or after it.

On its own it is small, but a contract amendment is not something that is usually thrown away. If Kojo was clearing out a draft they had finished with, it is explained.
tell.8:
At {t:07:20} on Saturday 17 October, the Security log on {m:OPS-07} was cleared by a program {p:Ama} had started. That log is the machine's own record of who signed in and what they changed, so clearing it wipes the history anyone would use to check what happened there.

Nothing else unusual was seen around it. An administrator clearing a full log on purpose would explain it, so it is worth asking Ama whether they meant to.
tell.10: Between {t:05:19} and {t:05:20} on Thursday 15 October, two nightly backup images, {f:nightly-0.vhdx} and {f:nightly-1.vhdx}, and the spreadsheet {f:plan0.xlsx} were deleted on {m:LOG-02}, where {p:Abena} signs in. Backups being removed is what drew attention to it.
